item.text: I’ll read the two supplied brief files, create the requested TSV, and check only that file’s formatting.

item.aggregated_output:
Read /Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec12/luna/package.md. It holds image section 12 (Sıkı dokuma, yerine oturan kapı ve örümceğin evi) of the frozen surah commentary of surah 103: the Arabic text of the ayat concerned, the Turkish
commentary written on them, the words/roots/branch labels recorded in the frozen surah commentary, and the
whole surah in Arabic. The selected commentary defines your scope; the other inputs supply context.

Find, from the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament, and the Jewish and Christian literature around them (Targum,
Mishnah, Talmud, midrash, pseudepigrapha, Christian apocrypha, Church Fathers, Syriac homilies), every text an
advanced reader of this commentary should have beside it. Judge each text on what it says in its own place, not
on resemblance of a word. Weigh at least:

- paralel: the same figure, scene or story told in the other scripture;
- motif: a shared image, formula, liturgical act or ethical motif without a shared story;
- karsi_anlati: the Qur'an tells it differently, corrects or answers it; the difference is the point;
- soydas: a Hebrew, Aramaic or Syriac cognate of a key word of these ayat and how the other scripture uses it;
- yorum_gelenegi: Jewish or Christian interpretation of a parallel text that changes what the parallel means.

Before grading, work through every distinct scene, object, action, relation, formula and secondary sense
actually developed in the commentary, including any v16 augment additions. Recall direct formulations, repeated
occurrences, nonlexical parallels, relevant reversals and interpretive traditions. Do not let the title, first
scene or already quoted passages stand in for the whole page. For a Buluşmalar section, consider the particular
meetings between images its prose develops. Root/branch labels are not dictionary definitions, evidence of
cognacy or permission to import an undeveloped sense. Do this review internally; output only candidate rows.

Use the package's Semitic root table: for every Arabic root it lists, recall how the corresponding Hebrew or
Aramaic root is used across the Hebrew Bible, passages that play on the same consonants, and passages whose
wording shows a difference from what the ayah says. Propose such passages as soydas (shared root), motif,
paralel or karsi_anlati as fits, and name the basis in `basis` (the root, and whether it is the table's sound
correspondence or your own recollection). Same consonants with an unrelated sense are not a connection.

Every explanation must identify a particular detail or claim in the commentary, the corresponding detail in
the candidate's own context, and what the relationship adds. Shared vocabulary, a broad religious theme or
the same speaker alone is insufficient. Do not invent imagery that neither text supports. A shared word is
not required. Preserve indirect, secondary and contrary readings with a concrete connection; do not choose
one preferred reading. A parallel is not a dependence: say what the texts share, not who borrowed.

Check the speaker, addressee, action, negation and verse boundary in remembered context. Name a neighbouring
verse separately when its own contribution is necessary; proximity alone does not qualify it. Keep Hebrew,
Aramaic, Syriac and Greek quotations short and specific to the cited passage and witness. If exact wording or
numbering is uncertain, explain the connection and uncertainty in English instead of reconstructing a quote.
Label roots, dictionary forms and wording from the source commentary explicitly. Never combine verses into
one quotation. Distinguish WLC's written/ketiv stream from qere and other readings; name another witness when
you rely on it. Discovery is memory-only: the later verifier will open the actual texts and check your claims.

Include every candidate meeting this standard. There is no target list length. Strong means a direct,
specific correspondence, including a secondary feature developed in the prose. Medium means a specific
correspondence with an explicit interpretive bridge. Weak means a plausible, specific connection whose
uncertainty you identify; it still cannot be generic. Counter-narrative is a relationship kind, not weaker
confidence. Model agreement and a follow-up origin never make a claim verified.

Write one TSV row per distinct connection with exactly six tab-separated fields:

strength	tradition	kind	ref	basis	short_explanation

strength: strong, medium, weak. tradition: tevrat (Hebrew Bible and Jewish literature) or incil (New Testament and
Christian literature). kind: paralel, motif, karsi_anlati, soydas, yorum_gelenegi. ref: for the Hebrew Bible and
the New Testament an edition-qualified OSIS reference, one verse per row, no ranges
(WLC:Gen.22.2, WLC:Ps.1.3, SBLGNT:Matt.6.5; consecutive verses on their own rows).
Use Hebrew WLC numbering for Hebrew Bible candidates and SBLGNT numbering for New Testament candidates;
do not silently transfer English/KJV verse numbers. For other works give the work and its place as a reader
cites it (Targum Jonathan on Genesis 22:2;
Genesis Rabbah 56:1; Berakhot 60b; Ephrem, Hymns on Paradise 5:6; Protevangelium of James 8). basis: the words,
scene or motif that carries the link, in a few words. Strongest first. Keep distinct reasons or link kinds for
one passage in separate rows; exact repeated connections are unnecessary. Do not regrade an existing row.
The handoff groups references but preserves each distinct connection for an individual verdict.

Do not write a header row, rank numbers, Markdown, sections or prose outside TSV rows. Save the rows to
/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec12/luna/list.tsv. End nonempty files with a newline. Zero qualifying candidates means an explicitly created
empty file. The saved file, not the chat response, is the deliverable.

## Frozen commentary (Turkish)

İplik sıkı dokunur: {ar:ثوب محقق إذا كان محكم النسج, tr:sevbun muhakkak, gloss:sağlam dokunmuş kumaş, source:"ح ق ق,B010"}; söz sağlam kurulur {ar:كلام محقق أي رصين, tr:kelâmun muhakkak, gloss:sağlam söz, source:"ح ق ق,B010"}; kapının ayağı yuvasına oturur {ar:مطابقة رجل الباب في حقه, tr:mutâbakatu ricli'l-bâb fî hakkıh, gloss:kapının ayağının yuvasına uyması, source:"ح ق ق,B011"}; iki kemiğin buluştuğu yer de haktır {ar:الحق ملتقى كل عظمين, tr:el-hakku multekâ kulli azmeyn, gloss:hak, iki kemiğin buluşma yeri, source:"ح ق ق,B011"}. Binada kerpiç kullanılır {ar:والبناء يستعمل اللبن, tr:ve'l-bennâu yesta'milu'l-lebin, gloss:yapı ustası kerpiç kullanır, source:"ع م ل,B002"}; bozulan onarılır {ar:الصلاح ضد الفساد والاصلاح نقيض الإفساد, tr:el-islâhu nakîdu'l-ifsâd, gloss:onarmak bozmanın karşıtıdır, source:"ص ل ح,B001"}; parça parçaya eklenir {ar:ووصيت الشيء وصلته, tr:vasaytu'ş-şey', gloss:şeyi bağladım, source:"و ص ي,B001"}. Karşıtı da aynı kelimededir: örümceğin evi hak diye anılır: {ar:حق الكهول بيت العنكبوت, tr:hakku'l-kuhûl, gloss:"hakku'l-kuhûl" örümcek evidir, source:"ح ق ق,B011"}.

Bu sahnede üçüncü ayetin dört kelimesi bir yapıyı kurar: iş kerpici koyar, salih bozuğu onarır, tavsiye parçaları ekler, hak dokumayı sıklaştırır ve kapıyı yerine oturtur. Düz anlatım hakkın sağlamlık, sıkılık ve yerine oturma olduğunu göstermez. Kur'an bozmayı, eklenmesi emredileni kesmeyi ve kaybı tek ayette birleştirir: {ar:ٱلَّذِينَ يَنقُضُونَ عَهْدَ ٱللَّهِ مِنۢ بَعْدِ مِيثَٰقِهِۦ وَيَقْطَعُونَ مَآ أَمَرَ ٱللَّهُ بِهِۦٓ أَن يُوصَلَ وَيُفْسِدُونَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ۚ أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْخَٰسِرُونَ, tr:ellezîne yenkudûne ahdallâhi ... ve yaktaûne mâ emerallâhu bihî en yûsale ve yufsidûne fi'l-ard, ulâike humu'l-hâsirûn, gloss:Allah'ın ahdini pekiştirdikten sonra bozan, Allah'ın bağlanmasını emrettiğini kesen ve yeryüzünde bozgunculuk yapanlar; işte kaybedenler onlardır, source:2:27}. Burada kaybın karşısında tam olarak üçüncü ayetin işleri durur: bağlamak, ıslah etmek. Bozulan iplik de Kur'an'da bir misaldir: {ar:وَلَا تَكُونُوا۟ كَٱلَّتِى نَقَضَتْ غَزْلَهَا مِنۢ بَعْدِ قُوَّةٍ أَنكَٰثًۭا, tr:ve lâ tekûnû kelletî nekadat gazlehâ, gloss:ipliğini sağlamca büktükten sonra çözüp lime lime eden kadın gibi olmayın, source:16:92}. Sağlam yapı da anılır: {ar:كَأَنَّهُم بُنْيَٰنٌۭ مَّرْصُوصٌۭ, tr:keennehum bunyânun marsûs, gloss:sanki birbirine kenetlenmiş bir yapı, source:61:4}, ve temel karşılaştırılır: {ar:أَم مَّنْ أَسَّسَ بُنْيَٰنَهُۥ عَلَىٰ شَفَا جُرُفٍ هَارٍۢ فَٱنْهَارَ بِهِۦ فِى نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ, tr:em men essese bunyânehû alâ şefâ curufin hâr, gloss:yoksa binasını çökmekte olan bir yarın kenarına kurup onunla birlikte cehennem ateşine yuvarlanan mı, source:9:109}. Örümceğin evi de Allah'tan başkasını dost edinenlerin misalidir: {ar:وَإِنَّ أَوْهَنَ ٱلْبُيُوتِ لَبَيْتُ ٱلْعَنكَبُوتِ, tr:ve inne evhene'l-buyûti le-beytu'l-ankebût, gloss:evlerin en çürüğü örümceğin evidir, source:29:41}.

## Whole surah (Arabic)

103:2	إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ لَفِى خُسْرٍ
103:3	إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلصَّبْرِ

item.text: The commentary develops construction, fit, bodily joining, sound speech, mutual advice, and the spider’s weak house. I’m carrying those separate links into the TSV, including the root-table correspondences with their uncertainty stated.

item.command:
/bin/bash -lc "cat > enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec12/luna/list.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.122.3	built city joined together	The commentary says parts are joined into a firm whole; Psalm 122 calls Jerusalem a city built and compactly joined together, giving that construction image a communal form.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Neh.4.6	joined wall; people minded to work	The commentary makes work lay bricks and counsel join pieces; Nehemiah says the wall was joined together while the whole people had a mind to work, uniting labor and assembly in one scene.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.26.19	frame tenons received by silver sockets	The commentary’s door foot fitting its socket has a precise joinery counterpart in the tabernacle frames, whose tenons sit over paired silver sockets; the image is exact fitting rather than a loose attachment.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.26.6	curtains clasped into one tabernacle	The commentary glosses counsel as connecting one thing to another; Exodus describes woven curtains fastened by clasps so they become one tabernacle, making joining a concrete act of assembly.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.37.7	bones came together bone to bone	The commentary calls the meeting place of bones haqq; in Ezekiel’s vision the dry bones come together bone to bone before sinews and flesh return, turning that junction into the first step of bodily restoration.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Eph.4.16	body held together by joints; each part works	The commentary joins work, repair, and fitted parts in one structure; Ephesians describes a body joined through its joints, with each part working as it should so the whole builds itself up.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Eph.4.25	speak truth to neighbor; members of one another	The commentary makes mutual counsel connect people; Ephesians tells each person to speak truth with a neighbor because they are members of one another, joining truthful speech to communal interdependence.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Zech.8.16	speak truth each to neighbor	The commentary’s repeated mutual counsel in truth is directly echoed by Zechariah’s instruction to speak truth to one another and judge truthfully for peace in the gates.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.15.2	does righteousness and speaks truth in the heart	The commentary places righteous action beside truthful counsel; Psalm 15 describes the person who does righteousness and speaks truth inwardly, joining ethical conduct and truth in one portrait.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.12.19	truthful lips endure; lying tongue is momentary	The commentary calls haqq a weighty, sound word; Proverbs says truthful lips stand forever while a lying tongue lasts only a moment, making durability an effect of truthful speech.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.4.12	threefold cord not quickly broken	The commentary develops tightly woven thread and pieces made secure by joining; Ecclesiastes says a threefold cord is not quickly snapped, a direct image of strength through strands joined together.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.24	stir one another to love and good works	The commentary’s mutual counsel connects people in constructive action; Hebrews asks readers to consider one another and stir each other toward love and good works, making that reciprocity explicitly ethical.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.5.11	encourage and build one another up	The commentary says counsel joins parts into a sound structure; Paul tells the community both to encourage one another and to build one another up, transferring the construction image to mutual support.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1John.3.18	love in deed and truth	The commentary puts work and haqq together in a constructive account; 1 John says love must be shown in deed and truth, pairing action with truth while warning against speech alone.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.7.24	house on rock; hears and does the words	The commentary sets sound construction against a weak house; Jesus’ wise builder hears and does his words and builds on rock, making practiced teaching the secure foundation.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.41.6	neighbors help and urge one another	The commentary makes mutual counsel connect and strengthen parts; Isaiah depicts people helping a neighbor and telling a brother to be strong, a concrete scene of reciprocal strengthening.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.8.14	spider’s house as failed confidence	The commentary names the spider’s house as the opposite of what is sound and well-fitted; Job compares a godless person’s confidence to a spider’s house, explicitly making that dwelling an image of unreliable refuge.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.59.6	spider webs cannot serve as clothing or cover	The commentary contrasts firm weaving with the spider’s insubstantial house; Isaiah says the webs woven by wrongdoers cannot become garments or cover them, giving the web a specific failure as protective fabric.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.28.17	justice as line; righteousness as plumb line	The commentary’s fitting door and sound construction make correctness spatially exact; Isaiah measures with justice and righteousness and says hail sweeps away a refuge of lies, connecting moral truth, proper alignment, and a failed shelter.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.24.3	house built by wisdom and established by understanding	The commentary’s builder’s work produces a structure made sound; Proverbs says wisdom builds a house and understanding establishes it, an explicit pairing of construction with stability.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.4.10	one lifts the companion who falls	The commentary makes mutual counsel connect separate parts; Ecclesiastes says one companion can lift the other after a fall, giving that connection a practical form of repair and support.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.19.17	reprove neighbor rather than bear sin	The commentary’s repeated counsel concerns people correcting and joining one another; Leviticus commands frank reproof of a neighbor to prevent sin, a specific ethical form of corrective counsel.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.3.13	exhort one another daily against deception	The commentary makes mutual counsel part of a sound communal structure; Hebrews calls for daily mutual exhortation so no one is hardened by sin’s deceit, showing counsel as protection against moral failure.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.14.19	pursue peace and mutual upbuilding	The commentary’s joining image treats connection as constructive; Paul tells the community to pursue peace and what builds one another up, making the goal of connection communal edification.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Jer.22.13	house built by injustice and unpaid labor	The commentary’s work and repair make a sound structure; Jeremiah condemns a ruler who builds his house through unrighteousness and unpaid labor, exposing a building that embodies injustice rather than repair.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.11.3	baked bricks and bitumen mortar	The commentary says the builder uses mudbrick; the Babel builders make fired bricks and use bitumen for mortar, a concrete ancient building parallel whose surrounding story gives collective construction a different aim.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Gen.11.4	building to make a name and avoid scattering	The commentary’s joined parts belong to a constructive moral community; Babel’s builders seek a name for themselves and fear being scattered, making their unity an ambitious self-protective project rather than the commentary’s ethical repair.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Gen.11.8	the builders are scattered	The commentary presents joining as a way to repair and secure; after Babel’s construction, God scatters the builders, a reversal in which a project meant to hold people together ends in dispersal.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Ezek.13.10	wall coated over a claim of peace	The commentary calls speech sound when it is firmly founded; Ezekiel condemns prophets who say “peace” when there is no peace while people build a wall and coat it with whitewash, joining false speech to a deceptive structure.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Ezek.13.11	whitewashed wall falls in storm	The commentary contrasts secure construction with a weak house; Ezekiel predicts that the whitewashed wall will fall under flooding rain and hail, exposing a façade that cannot hold.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.59.5	spider webs woven by wrongdoers	The commentary juxtaposes firm weaving with the spider’s weak dwelling; Isaiah says wrongdoers weave spider webs, linking the spider image to destructive rather than protective work.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.7.26	house built on sand	The commentary contrasts firm, fitted construction with a fragile shelter; Jesus’ foolish builder puts his house on sand, specifying the unstable foundation behind failure.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.7.27	house collapses with a great fall	The commentary contrasts a sound structure with a weak house; Jesus says the sand-built house falls when storm waters and winds strike, making collapse the consequence of a bad foundation.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.10	builder lays a foundation and must take care how he builds	The commentary makes construction an image for coordinated action; Paul describes himself as a skilled builder who laid a foundation and warns each builder to take care, making workmanship and responsibility explicit.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.12	gold, stone, wood, hay, straw as building materials	The commentary distinguishes sound construction from the spider’s weak house; Paul lists materials of sharply different durability for what people build, making the quality of the work consequential.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.13	each person’s work is tested by fire	The commentary links work to a structure that can hold or fail; Paul says fire will disclose and test each builder’s work, adding an explicit test of what construction can endure.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.2.5	living stones built into a spiritual house	The commentary turns building and joined pieces into a moral image; 1 Peter calls its readers living stones being built into a spiritual house, giving communal construction a religious interpretation.
medium	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Matt.7.26	hears words but does not do them	The commentary contrasts constructive deeds with a weak house; Jesus’ foolish builder hears but does not do the words, and so builds on sand, making the missing practice the moral fault behind the unstable structure.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.127.1	עָמָל ~ ع م ل; table’s regular sound correspondence, unverified	Psalm 127 says that without YHWH building the house, its builders עָמָלוּ, “toil,” in vain; this matches the commentary’s builder using brick through a possible root correspondence while stressing that labor alone can be futile.
